introduction-who-are-you-and-what-can-yo.core: IAM answers two questions for every API call: authentication (who are you: a user, role or federated identity) and authorisation (what can you do: policies allowing or denying actions on resources under conditions). Every AWS request is evaluated this way.

first_principles.problem: Teams share long-lived access keys with admin rights, and a leaked key compromises everything.
truths: Every API call is signed and evaluated.

analogy.title: A building with ID badges and door permissions
analogy.story: Your badge says who you are; door rules say where you can go.
analogy.breaks: Badges are physical; credentials can be stolen and used from anywhere unless conditions restrict them.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Leaked credentials can only read reports.

points: Who are you, what can you do.

check.q: Why prefer IAM roles over IAM users' access keys?
check.a: Roles provide temporary, automatically rotated credentials, reducing the impact of leaks.

the-core-logic-how-aws-decides-policy-ev.core: AWS starts from implicit deny. An explicit Deny anywhere wins. Otherwise access requires an Allow, and every applicable boundary (SCPs, resource control policies, permission boundaries, session policies) must also allow. Identity and resource policies combine (within an account either can allow). Cross-account access needs both sides to allow.

first_principles.problem: A user has AdministratorAccess but still gets AccessDenied, and nobody knows why.
derivation: Check **identity or resource policy** allows it.
Cross-account: **both** identity and resource policies must allow.

analogy.title: A nightclub entry check
analogy.story: You need to be on the guest list, pass the dress code and age check, and anyone on the banned list is refused outright.
analogy.breaks: Bouncers can make exceptions; IAM evaluation is deterministic.

steps.label: Tool
steps.detail: IAM Policy Simulator and the error's 'explicit deny in SCP' message.

check.q: Can an identity policy Allow override an SCP Deny?
check.a: No: an explicit deny anywhere, including an SCP, always wins.

service-control-policies-scps-the-organi.core: SCPs are AWS Organizations policies attached to the root, OUs or accounts that set the maximum permissions for all principals in those accounts (except the management account). They grant nothing themselves; they restrict, e.g. deny leaving the organisation, disabling CloudTrail or using unapproved regions.

first_principles.problem: A developer with admin rights in a sandbox account disables CloudTrail and launches resources in unapproved regions.
truths: Account admins can do anything their policies allow.
Org-level guardrails need to bind admins too.
derivation: Common guardrails: **region restriction**, **protect CloudTrail/Config**, **deny root actions**, **deny leaving org**.

analogy.title: A national constitution
analogy.story: Local governments can make laws, but none can override constitutional limits.
analogy.breaks: Constitutions grant rights; SCPs only ever restrict.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Even admins can't launch in us-east-1; global services exempted.

check.q: Does an SCP apply to the organisation's management account?
check.a: No, which is why the management account should be tightly controlled and not run workloads.

permission-boundaries-the-sandbox-for-de.core: A permission boundary is a managed policy attached to a user or role that caps its maximum permissions. It lets you delegate IAM role creation to developers safely: they can create roles only if those roles carry the same boundary, preventing privilege escalation.

first_principles.problem: Developers need to create roles for their Lambda functions, but could create an admin role and escalate.
truths: Delegated admins can escalate without limits.
Conditions can require a boundary on created roles.

analogy.title: A company credit card with a spending limit
analogy.story: You can buy what you need, and any card you issue to your team has the same limit.
analogy.breaks: Credit limits are monetary; boundaries limit actions and resources.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Devs self-serve roles, never beyond DevBoundary.

check.q: What are a role's effective permissions with a boundary?
check.a: The intersection of its identity policies and its permission boundary.

cross-account-roles-trusting-strangers-s.core: Cross-account access uses a role in the target account whose trust policy allows a principal from the source account to call sts:AssumeRole. The source principal also needs permission to assume it. For third parties, require an ExternalId to prevent the confused-deputy problem.

first_principles.problem: A SaaS vendor needs read access to your account without you handing over access keys.
truths: Trust and permissions are separate policies.
Temporary credentials are safer than keys.
Vendors serving many customers can be tricked into acting for the wrong one.
derivation: Create a **role in the target account**.

analogy.title: A guest key with a passphrase
analogy.story: The building lets a named company in, but only if they quote your unique passphrase.
analogy.breaks: Physical keys don't expire; role sessions do, typically within 1–12 hours.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Only the vendor, acting for you, can assume the role.

check.a: The confused deputy, where another customer tricks the vendor into using its access to your account.

abac-attribute-based-access-control.core: ABAC grants access based on matching tags: a principal tagged team=payments can access resources tagged team=payments, using conditions like aws:ResourceTag/team == ${aws:PrincipalTag/team}. One policy scales across teams and new resources without editing policies for each.

first_principles.problem: Every new project needs new IAM policies listing ARNs, and the policy count explodes.
truths: Conditions can compare principal and resource tags.

analogy.title: Colour-coded keycards and doors
analogy.story: A blue card opens every blue door, including doors built tomorrow.
analogy.breaks: Colours can't be repainted by holders, but tags can be changed unless you deny it.

check.q: Why must you prevent users from changing resource tags under ABAC?
check.a: Retagging a resource with their own team tag would grant them access to it.
